title: Gambling Crackdown Rocks the NBA, AWS Stumbles, and MTV’s Music Era Ends
text:
A sweeping FBI probe into illegal sports betting landed dozens of arrests that include high-profile NBA names, MTV winding down several international music channels, and Amazon’s cloud keeps going down while your subscription prices keep going up, and Texas teams own the AP Top 25. Let’s dig in.

 MTV Shuts Down Music Channels Outside Of US 

 MTV was once a cultural juggernaut, captivating audiences and shaping culture for the younger generation through music, and representing the authenticity of the human experience with their MTV Animation phase. MTV is pulling several of its music channels out of markets outside the U.S., a clear sign that scaled linear TV is on its last leg. 

 They say the way people consume content has changed. Which is true. Apparently they’re actually writing shows now, dumbing down the plot, explaining everything that’s happening in dialogue, because they know people will be on their phones while watching. That’s not the type of thing that breathes life into a story. No wonder over the last few decades it seems like the soul has been sucked out American media.

 I’m not gonna lie, I want the old MTV back. Going back and watching slice-of-life shows like Downtown, Daria, and Mission Hill *, take you back to a simpler time with more raw authenticity that’s missing from day-to-day life today. But cost and retention are real concerns when running a business, and being a profitable voice of a generation is hard. 

 MTV’s move to reality and viral TV is probably the reason the main network is still up and running today. Vice is another example. As a thing scales, it’s harder to maintain its essence. Smaller, nimble programming blocks like Adult Swim have survived by finding a fantastic partnership and not scaling; that model looks more sustainable than big-budget mass programming right now.

 AWS is down again 

 The internet hiccuped again when a major AWS problem took down big services multiple times last month. For a company that accounts for over 1% of US GDP , with over 1 million US employees, should have some level of accountability, or we should remove this single point of failure as a bottleneck. Their footprint is massive. They even have an effect on prices for streaming services. When AWS raises their prices, Netflix and other services pass that cost down to the customer. As Amazon cuts tens of thousands of employees and automates, which would have a material impact on our economy, some hard questions will have to be asked. 

 Sports 

 FBI arrests 30 NBA Players & Staff in Multiple Gambling Scandals 

 The FBI’s sweep led to more than 30 arrests tied to separate gambling investigations, and it includes high-profile names, including Portland coach and Hall of Famer Chauncey Billups and Miami Heat guard Terry Rozier.

 Prosecutors say Billups was involved in lavish, rigged poker games run by organized crime, with high-tech cheating tools that sound like something out of a movie: X-ray card tables, modified shufflers, chip-tray analyzers, and glasses or contact lenses that could reveal opponents’ cards. Federal filings allege the scheme defrauded players of millions. Allegedly, multiple mafia families are invovled. They’ll go after NBA stars, but they’re either too afraid of or too involved with the mafia to arrest them. 

 Rozier was arrested in connection with a separate sports-betting case. According to charging documents, investigators allege he shared confidential NBA information and tipped associates about in-game exits and other details that could be used to manipulate prop bets. He has been placed on leave while the case proceeds.

 Adam Silver has warned publicly about the “dire risks” gambling poses to the integrity of the game. The cases and concerns come just as the NCAA decided to allow college athletes to bet on sports. They had to push back the effective date for the rule change to November 22, after blowback from coaches and conferences worried about integrity. 

 Texas Takes Over AP Top 25

 Speaking of college sports, Texas is flexing: multiple programs remain in the AP Top 25 and new teams are pushing for attention, and Texas is the only state with 4 teams on the list. The regular-season matchups coming in November could reshape the picture, so keep an eye on UNT and the big Texas clash with A&M later this month.

title: Prediction Markets Go Mainstream, AI Dominates GDP Growth, & The Middle Class Is At Risk
text:
The middle class is at risk. Let’s be real.

 The post-Covid bounce in the economy was short lived. Inflation eventually caught up to consumers. Shareholders’ appetite for relentless growth has driven shrinkflation, and an AI push could result in large firms that operate with far fewer people than before. I explored that trend in my last piece on AI and the Social Contract .

 You can see the contradiction everywhere. Stock indexes have been hitting record highs while hiring and planned hiring are weakening, with some measures of hiring at levels we haven’t seen since the Great Recession . When asset prices and labor market signals pull in different directions, the middle is the squeeze point.

 

 

 McDonald’s CEO Chris Kempczinski warned on CNBC that “it’s really kind of a two-tier economy,” noting that upper-income households (roughly those earning over $100k) are seeing different effects than middle and lower-income consumers. Bank of America’s October 2025 Consumer Checkpoint report backs that up. It highlights a clear gap in spending growth and financial resilience between higher and lower-income households. A “tale of two wallets,” as they put it.

 Walk the grocery aisle and the proof hits you in the cart: packages are smaller while prices stay the same or go up. That’s shrinkflation, and it has been on the rise since 2021 as companies trim size or servings to hold prices steady.

 If the currency and asset dynamics push more of the next generation away from homeownership while top 10% grows their asset power, we need practical escape hatches for the bottom 90%. That’s where micro-economies come in.

 A Texas Lens on The Issue 

 This two-tier squeeze is visible across Texas, from big metros to smaller neighborhoods. In Houston, the closure of Funplex in Alief this year is a blunt example. The nearly 200,000 square foot family entertainment center shuttered and auctioned off arcade cabinets, go-karts and props; a casualty of rising operating costs and weaker attendance for big footprint, mid-market venues. That kind of loss isn’t just nostalgic, it’s an economic signal. Family-oriented third spaces already run on thin margins, and they’re the first to disappear when the middle class starts to shrink.

 Houston’s restaurant landscape shows the same pressure. Longstanding staples like Picos & Razzoo’s have closed or gone bankrupt , showing that beloved local spots can be pushed under by rising rent, wages and insurance. Meanwhile, luxury retail and high-end restaurants in well-heeled neighborhoods prosper. From the colorful houses that used to line Rainey St. in Austin, to local entertainment like Peter Pan Mini-golf (Austin) and Funplex, there has to be a way to sustain the establishments that give our neighborhoods character.

 Think Micro 

 Micro-economies are not a radical idea. They are a practical hedge against centralized, extractive scale. The modern economy is increasingly made of these niche markets built around specialized communities and interests. The internet era has unlocked novel ways to create value, built on top of existing industries, loyalty, trust, and fandom. They come in all shapes and sizes and can graduate with mainstream adoption. 

 Modern creators and streamers on platforms like YouTube and Twitch can turn audience engagement into income. Savvy card collectors can monetize their fandom. Traders can turn their knowledge into profit in prediction markets. Every micro-economy is an economic release valve.

 In effect, micro-economies provide diversification and new income streams that more people can tap into. As traditional jobs become less secure, fans and creators rely on these alternative asset classes to survive and thrive. I discuss this more in The Case for Microeconomies .

 Prediction Markets Are Here To Stay 

 

 

 Prediction markets are not a fringe toy anymore. They’ve had their iPhone moment. Shows, streamers, sports broadcasters, and major exchange operators are now part of the story.

 South Park even ran an episode about them and Tom Brady name-dropped Polymarket on a live NFL broadcast. Prediction markets let you bet on anything from how long the government shutdown will last to how many views Mr. Beast gets on his next video. The notoriety and the volume on these apps are way up.

 The story of Polymarket, the largest on-chain prediction market plays like a movie. Last year, federal agents raided Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan’s home , seizing electronics in an investigation into them allowing US users on their platform before they got a license. Just a year later, Intercontinental Exchange, owner of the New York Stock Exchange, moved to invest up to $2 billion in Polymarket . They now have a license to operate in the US.

 Prediction markets raise big questions: market integrity, regulatory frameworks, manipulation risk, and whether information markets improve forecasting or just monetize noise.

 AI Acceleration 

 AI is reshaping work, education, and culture, fast. Experiments like Alpha School ’s two-hour learning model show how adaptive software can turbocharge outcomes in boutique settings, but the price and scalability questions are real.

 ChatGPT recently hit ~800M weekly active users, a reminder of how ubiquitous these tools have become. And it’s being used in crucial circumstances. A Top US Army general says he’s using ChatGPT to help make key command decisions . AI is almost guaranteed to make mistakes given enough time on a task. Consulting giant Deloitte has agreed to refund part of a $290,000 consultancy fee to the Australian government after admitting that a report it delivered, which included AI-generated content, was riddled with fabricated citations and misattributions. We must take care when we use these tools, and remember that AI multiplies productivity if you supervise it, and multiplies mistakes if you don’t.

 Are We In an AI Bubble? 

 Harvard economist Jason Furman has warned that U.S. GDP growth in the first half of 2025 is being propped up by data center investments. Without them the U.S. would’ve been at a measly 0.1% GDP growth. Growth concentrated in a tiny slice of the economy can leave most sectors exposed if that spending slows.

 Sports 

 A new study from the University of Texas at El Paso finds that officiating calls from 2015–2023 disproportionately favored the Kansas City Chiefs in high-leverage moments, a claim that has reignited long-running debates about parity and the theater of officiating. Back in February, The NFL referees association pushed back hard, calling bias claims were “insulting” and stressing weekly performance reviews and grading of crews. Whether anything has changed is up for debate, with instances of inconsistent taunting calls and missed or called-back OPI flags in recent weeks. 

 This week Texas A&M (#4), Texas Tech (#7), and Texas (#21) are all ranked in the AP Top 25 , a great moment for the Texas. Both the Red Raiders are 6–0 and Texas A&M are 6–0 and it’s their best starts in over a decade. The last time Texas had 3 teams ranked was in 2011 (Baylor, Texas, and A&M). Texas and Tennessee are the only states with three teams currently ranked, and Florida and Alabama are the only other states to have achieved this feat.

title: AI & The Social Contract: Competing Visions For Our Future
text:
Last month, a small town museum in Ohio advertised a single opening for an administrative assistant. Within forty‑eight hours more than four hundred résumés poured in: from mid‑career librarians displaced by digital catalogues to fresh graduates hunting for a first paycheck. Their desperation is not an isolated event. The New York Fed pegs recent‑graduate unemployment at 5.8% , while Oxford Economics finds that entry‑level tech posts are vanishing fastest of all.

 Artificial intelligence has poured jet fuel on a slide the American middle class has been riding for half a century. The debate is no longer whether we need a new social contract—it is whose vision will set its terms.

 Innovative Hype is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

 

 

 

 OpenAI’s mission is “to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity.” Yet the guardrails that might guarantee broad dividends remain hazy. If public institutions can’t keep pace, how do we hold AI giants accountable, and how do we keep the promise of the American Dream alive for ordinary workers?

 

 The Slow‑Motion Unraveling of the Middle Class 

 In 1970, working‑class families captured roughly 62 cents of every U.S. dollar created. By 2020 their share had slipped to 42 cents . Wealth, meanwhile, has consolidated upstream. The top 10% now own 93% of all stocks. Even six‑figure earners feel the squeeze: almost half live paycheck to paycheck, and one in five households making $150 k still juggle grocery bills against mortgage payments. Instead of getting ahead, families now watch their savings stall, their dream of buying a house fade, and their daily finances drift into a constant state of emergency management.

 

 Two Diverging AI Philosophies 

 Sam Altman: Rewrite the Contract 

 At Geneva’s AI for Good Summit last May, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman argued that the potency of frontier models would eventually “require some change to the social contract” as society re‑tools safety nets for an era of abundant machine labor. He has floated ideas ranging from universal basic income to " universal basic compute "—fancy jargon for a free plan once they achieve AGI ( Artificial General Intelligence , refers to an AI system with the ability to perform any intellectual task that a human can—i.e. we don’t need humans anymore).

 Dario Amodei: Preserve the Contract 

 Last week, on Anderson Cooper 360 , Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei struck a different chord: 

 “There’s an inherent social contract in democracy where the ordinary person has leverage because they’re contributing to the economy. If that leverage goes away, it’s harder to keep democracy itself working.” 

 Amodei urged lawmakers to contemplate targeted AI taxes and profit‑sharing before inequality metastasizes:

 “ I wouldn’t exclude the notion of levying a tax on AI companies. If AI creates huge total wealth, a lot of that will by default go to AI companies and less to ordinary people. Definitely not in my interest to say that, but I think this is something we should consider and I think it shouldn’t be partisan“

 Why the Distinction Matters 

 Both leaders concede that generative AI eventually will vaporize broad bands of entry‑level knowledge work. Amodei projects that up to 50% of such jobs could disappear within five years—about one‑fifth of the entire U.S. workforce—an unprecedented outcome for a developed nation, let alone a G7 member. The tension between rewriting and safeguarding the social contract will shape whether AI deepens or diminishes democracy’s economic foundations.

 

 Power Accelerates, Institutions Lag 

 Inside Big Tech, AI already writes roughly a third of Google, Meta, and Microsoft’s production code; engineers at OpenAI and Anthropic give estimates closer to eighty percent on their own teams. Shopify’s Tobi Lütke tells employees to “prove AI can’t do the job before we hire” and there's a race to own the most AI agents—Salesforce's CEO Marc Benioff vows his company will be “the No. 1 digital labor provider, period,” while Google and Meta are " creating one million AI programmers " according to Eric Schmidt.

 The public sector can't keep up. U.S. K‑12 curricula update every six years while foundation models leap generations every six months. A two‑year‑old micro‑school in Texas, built around AI tutors, already ranks in the top two percent of state exams on two hours of daily instruction proof that yesterday’s classroom template is obsolete.

 

 Historical Flashpoints 

 Past technological shocks show that bold policy can ease dislocation. Britain’s Factory Acts limited child labor and capped brutal hours within a decade of the power loom’s spread. Germany’s Bismarck launched employer‑supported health and pension insurance in the 1880s to stabilize an industrializing society. The lesson: waiting for market forces alone to self‑correct invites Dickensian outcomes.

 

 Revival Playbooks 

  Medici‑Style Patronage (Top‑Down) 

 Fifteenth‑century Florence funneled roughly seventeen percent of Medici Bank profits into public art and engineering, financing cathedral worksites that employed three percent of the city. Dario's AI tax could be a modern parallel, caching one to five percent of gross AI revenue into a National Workforce Transition Fund. This mirrors Britain’s apprenticeship levy by financing stipends, retraining, and seed capital for worker‑owned startups.

 Supplemental levers include data‑royalty trusts (citizens share in model‑training proceeds) and profit‑linked tax rebates for firms that devote at least five percent of earnings to employee dividends.

  Loaves‑and‑Fish Micro‑Economies (Bottom‑Up) 

 Grass‑roots experiments already hint at local resilience. A Denver tech‑workers guild routes contracts through an AI matchmaker and keeps ninety‑two percent of fees in member pockets, Brooklyn’s DataUnion licensed community‑owned data for $4.2 million in 2024, and Detroit’s OpenFactory lets former auto workers co‑own modular AI‑driven production lines, boosting wages by twenty‑two percent. These micro‑economies recycle profits instead of siphoning them to distant boards.

 

 Rethinking Layoffs in Real Time 

 Not every company that replaced humans with chatbots is celebrating. Klarna axed seven hundred support agents only to rehire when customer satisfaction tanked. IBM’s “ AskHR ” bot failed to handle nuanced disputes, forcing a partial rollback. A 2025 survey shows 52% of firms now regret hasty AI cuts. The moral: human agility, judgment, and empathy still underpin durable value.

 

 Call to Action 

 We stand at a fork: a renaissance of shared prosperity—or a gilded age of concentrated power. Should we change the social contract, as Sam Altman suggests, or save it, as Dario Amodei insists? The answer will hinge on citizens’ resolve to demand equitable stakes and on lawmakers’ courage to tether exponential technology to democratic values.

 The next decade will decide whether AI becomes the great leveler or the ultimate wedge. The choice, still, is ours.

title: Innovative Hype Roundup September 2024
text:
Business 

 

 FED Makes First Rate Cut Since COVID 

 This month, the Federal Reserve made its first interest rate cut since March 2020. The FED reduced its key interest rate by 50 basis points , half of 1%, bringing the rate down to a range of 4.75% to 5%. This decision follows a period of aggressive rate hikes aimed at taming inflation, which had peaked at 9.1% in 2022. With inflation now near the FED’s 2% year-over-year target, the central bank has turned its attention to supporting a weakening job market. Officials indicated that more rate cuts are likely before the year ends.

 While officials have been cautious about labeling the current economic state as a recession, data such as two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth suggests otherwise. This measure has been a reliable recession indicator since 1948, and denying it may appear more political than factual. Despite pushback from the White House, which highlights strong job growth, many economists and voters believe we entered a recession before 2022, as the U.S. also experienced two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth in 2020. The FED’s recent pivot to rate cuts indicates a shift toward stimulating growth, potentially signaling the start of the recovery phase.

 

 Texas Y’all 

 

 Elon Musk Furthers His Takeover Of Texas, Declaring Bastrop As HQ For Social Media Company X 

 If you didn’t know already, Elon Musk loves Texas for its tax laws and general regulatory landscape. In July, he vowed to move all his remaining companies here. Now, all but two of his companies (Neuralink & xAI) are either headquartered in Texas or have a significant Texas footprint. In all, his companies now own ~$2.5B worth of property across the state. This includes facilities used by Tesla, SpaceX, The Boring Company, and X (formerly Twitter). Some key properties include Tesla’s Austin Gigafactory, spanning 2,500 acres, SpaceX's Starbase in Boca Chica, and the multiple projects The Boring Company has around Austin and Bastrop which adds about 281 acres between the latter two.

 Additionally, Musk acquired ~6,500 acres around Bastrop to build a living community for his employees called Snailbrook. The Boring Company has already built Hyperloop Plaza, a community space in Bastrop that includes a bodega, coffee shop, salon, pickleball courts, and a bar coming soon.

 

 Texas Stock Exchange Announced 

 In June 2024, TXSE Group Inc. announced the creation of the Texas Stock Exchange (TXSE), based in Dallas, Texas. This new national exchange is set to compete with established giants like the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq, offering an alternative for companies looking to access equity capital markets. Backed by significant financial powerhouses such as BlackRock and Citadel Securities, the TXSE has raised $120 million in initial funding and aims to be fully operational by 2025.

 TXSE aims to differentiate itself by being more CEO-friendly, appealing to corporations frustrated by the growing regulatory burden on other major exchanges. Very Texas. The exchange will be fully electronic and will trade public companies, ETPs, ADRs. The launch reflects Texas’ growth as a business hub, with the state now home to more Fortune 500 companies than any other U.S. state!

 

 Tech 

 

 Quick AI News 

 OpenAI ironically takes steps to become for profit company with a potential $10 billion payday for Sam Altman, while their CTO & Chief Research Officer quit 

 Cursor, an AI-enabled IDE, is the best AI tool for coders that you can use with your favorite LLM, turning you into a 10X engineer. People have been putting out tutorials of how to use it, like this one. 

 RunwayML makes deal with Lionsgate to license its movies for training data in a big win for consumers 

 A man in North Carolina has been arrested for using bots to generate millions of streams for thousands of AI-generated songs he created. 

 EA Games showcases real-time text-to-video game concept at investor day 

 

 Telegram Changes Its Tone On Moderating Private Chats After CEO’s Arrest 

 Telegram has quietly removed language from its FAQ page saying private chats were protected and that “we do not process any requests related to them.” The change came after its CEO, Pavel Durov, was arrested in Paris by French officials for allegedly allowing “criminal activity to go on undeterred on the messaging app."

 Users have always been able to report messages, but French officials will likely not allow Pavel Durov to leave France until they feel like there is a robust process to remove content they deem illegal from the app.

 

 Mark Zuckerberg’s Rebrand & Meta’s Innovation 

 Mark Zuckerberg has gone through a transformation this summer, putting his past “robot with no personality” image behind him. Now he’s making bold statements, rocking oversized heavyweight tees and chains. At a tech summit this month, Zuckerberg vowed to stop apologizing for Meta’s past controversies focus on things within his control, like innovation. This stance has been received well by investors, and the stock has only gone up since.

 Meta is tackling VR, AR, and AI and are very competitive in all three, considering the competition. Meta has the most compelling VR product. Now it seems like they have the most compelling AR product in Orion. 

 Mark Zuckerberg effectively killed Snapchat when Instagram introduced Reels. Since their IPO, and subsequent buyout offer from Meta, Snapchat has struggled to maintain growth or momentum regarding users, revenue, and innovation.

 And now they two companies are going head to head again, with augmented reality. Meta’s glasses look like normal glasses while Snapchat’s look more like IMAX 3D glasses. You can compare the other options as well. Microsoft HoloLens and Magic Leap products are both ugly have completely lost steam. Meta has no competition. 

 And with AI, they have the most democratic product. Open sourcing Meta’s LLM Llama is something you’d expect a non-profit called OpenAI to do, but he’s the only one releasing new open source models.

 

 Sports 

 

 How Nike & The WNBA Are Downplaying The Caitlin Clark Effect 

 Caitlin Clark, who has reportedly been named WNBA rookie of the year, has been a transformational figure for the WNBA. Her presence on the court has led to record-breaking viewership , with the Indiana Fever becoming the most watched team in the league, averaging a whopping 1.19 million viewers per game compared to the league’s average of 394,000. That’s a 300% increase. This massive following has even translated to increased betting on the WNBA​. “Consistent interest in Clark props and Fever moneylines, and a significant number of bets on the Fever outright make Clark’s influence on the league undeniable ,” BetMGM sports trader Hannah Luther said. Clark’s prop bets attracted more handle than any WNBA prop bets ever on Caesar’s Sportsbook.

 In response, some ex-players and ex-analysts for the WNBA have come out downlplay her dominance, including Sheryl Swoopes , Jemel Hill , and co-owner of the Atlanta Dream Renee Montgomery .

 Caitlin Clark signed an eight-year, $28 million endorsement deal with Nike, which includes a signature sneaker, This deal makes her one of the few women in history to receive a signature shoe. However, we haven’t seen any promotion of her by Nike as a pro. And the shoe might not come out until 2026, which limits Nike’s ability to capitalize on Clark’s arrival to the WNBA. Nike may be trying to avoid controversy by waiting until after Aj’a Wilson’s signature shoe drops, which is slated for 2025. 

 

 Was Tom Brady Right About NFL Rookie QBs Being Thrust Too Early Into The Fire? 

 The Carolina Panthers recent benching of sophomore Bryce Young, the No. 1 pick in the 2023 NFL Draft, after a challenging start to his NFL career, has reignited the debate about whether rookie quarterbacks are being thrown into starting roles too quickly.

 During a live recording of The Stephen A. Smith Show earlier this year, Brady reflected on his development trajectory as a quarterback . He emphasizes that for five years in college he got to learn gradually in a pro-style system, where he worked his way up from being the seventh quarterback on the depth chart to eventually starting. Then, in the NFL, he continued to develop for his rookie season, and didn’t start until game 3 of his sophomore season when Drew Bledsoe was injured. 

 The greatest quarterback of all time didn’t start a single game his rookie season. We shouldn’t expect more from anyone. This philosophy makes Arch Manning’s position at Texas make a lot more sense, but we’re still happy to see Arch get some good play time. 

 

 Big Ten, SEC to talk possible scheduling partnership 

 ESPN sources announced the SEC and Big Ten are meeting this week to discuss scheduling conversations. Creating similarities and somewhat equal competition between the two conferences is the goal of the Big Ten and SEC. As the two major conferences driving the conversation about CFP reform, the future of FBS continues to look like a two conference layout. What does this mean for the rest of the teams in the FBS? 

 Most in the conversation agree change is needed. 

 Playoff expansion and more structure 

 Automatic Bids from power conferences 

 Bowl game relevancy and criticism 

 Need to reform 

 Who is driving change? 

 Read this article for a more holistic idea of what the future of FBS should look like.

 

 Deion Sanders & The Colorado Buffaloes Bounce Back from A Lackluster 1st Season 

 Deion Sanders and the Colorado Buffaloes have shown significant improvement in the 2024 season, since their underwhelming 2023 campaign. After finishing 4-8 last year, they currently stand at 4-1, riding a three-game winning streak, including a dominant 48-21 victory over Central Florida. Travis Hunter has been a key factor, excelling on both sides of the ball and drawing Heisman attention for his performances. With the team now entering Big 12 play, Coach Prime has them on track for postseason contention, already matching last year’s win total. 

 

 Music

 

 Quick Music News 

 TikTok to Shutter Music Subscription Service TikTok Music in November 

 Spotify Beats Eminem Publisher’s Lawsuit Over Billions of Rapper’s Streams 

 Spotify Rolls Out Beta for Text-toPlaylist Feature 

 U.K. Government Steps in as Ticketmaster’s ‘Dynamic Pricing’ Fiasco triggers Public Outrage Over Surging Oasis Ticket Prices

title: The Case for Microeconomies
text:
You may be familiar with the term “ network state ,” but there's less discussion about its lesser-known sibling: the microeconomy. Microeconomies aren't a novel concept; people have been engaging in peer-to-peer transactions since the beginning of time. However, not much comes up when you search the term. The internet has supercharged these economies, exemplified by online gaming worlds like Runescape, World of Warcraft, and the burgeoning creator economy. With new technologies, these microeconomies are becoming easier to create and offer fresh avenues for generating value.

 In today's economy, the ability to turn nothing into something is more crucial than ever, with inflation running rampant. This conversation needs to be had now, as the benefits of being an early adopter are ripe, and the potential scale of these microeconomies is virtually unlimited. Their total addressable market is uncapped, presenting unprecedented opportunities.

 Innovative Hype is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

 

 

 

 

 Currency & Pre-internet 

 Before the internet, nobody could have imagined that being a blogger, streamer, YouTuber, or professional gamer could be viable careers. Yet, here we are in a thriving creator economy. In a recent podcast episode, Balaji Srinivasan, author of “ The Network State ” and host of The Network State podcast, highlighted the inherent value of micro-economies , using the Japanese Yen as an analogy:

 “The yen has value even if you’re not Japanese because enough Japanese people give it value. So if enough of those people coordinate they can build something amongst themselves even if the rest of the world doesn’t value it.” 

 -Balaji Srinivasan

 We get to choose what we value.

 

 The Internet & The Creator Economy 

 The internet era has unlocked novel ways to create value, transforming the very nature of value creation. We're moving away from traditional trickle-down economics to more experimental, bottom-up, and middle-out approaches. Microeconomies, in this sense, are the evolution of the creator economy – a new paradigm of value creation.

 

 Unlocking New Ways to Create Value 

 Virtual in-game marketplaces, internet platforms sharing ad revenue, and the broader creator economy are all examples of microeconomies. They extend the economy's market cap by introducing innovative ways to earn income. These microeconomies embody inclusiveness, offering more opportunities for people to support themselves, aligning with the ethos of web3 technologies like cryptocurrencies, DAOs, and NFTs. When we begin to value all our physical and digital possessions and create liquid markets around them, we break ourselves out of the “I can only buy this with X dollars” mentality as if we had a digital pawn shop everywhere we go. 

 

 Trickle-Down Economics to a Bottom-Up Approach 

 The Medici family's investment in the arts during the Renaissance demonstrates how supporting creativity can lead to significant societal impacts. Microeconomies represent an alternative to traditional models, offering new participants the chance to join emerging communities and contribute to their growth. You can invest in startup cities that may flourish in a few decades and startup currencies, several of which have grown to tens or hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap. You can also invest in budding artists early in their career and ride the waves as they gain notoriety.

 

 Examples of Successful Microeconomies 

 From game skins in CS:GO and Fortnite to the nostalgic surge in Pokémon card values, we see diverse manifestations of microeconomies. Time and time again, we’ve seen nascent microeconomies bud from an existing industry, creating new ways to monetize people’s interests. Each of these microeconomies innovated on top of an already established industry. Game skins are a $50 billion plus industry. Fantasy sports is a $10 billion industry in the US. The creator economy is worth $100 billion plus.

 Bitcoin's market cap is also a testament to the power of community-driven value. Microeconomies can even manifest in physical form. At pop-up events like Cooltopia at NFT NYC and DoodlePutt at Art Basel Miami, patrons run around and play games to generate tokens that can be redeemed for food, clothing, and accessories (let’s call these Proof-of-Fun experiences). These events demonstrate how alternative forms of currency can facilitate unique experiences that emphasize community buy-in and participation.

 

 Escape Valve + Join Your Cohort 

 One feature of microeconomies is that there are always new ones being created. Too much scale leads to corruption , and microeconomies create an escape valve for people who can’t exist in the current economy. Many of us take access to basic financial services for granted. In many countries, there are residents who do not have access to a bank account or other financial services, resulting from geography, lack of identification, or religious rules. Crypto offers an escape valve, allowing them to control their own money. Another benefit of new microeconomies popping up consistently is the ability to join your cohort. When a new microeconomy is created, the playing field is reset, allowing new users to participate without the pressure of existing participants who have been accumulating much longer. 

 

 In Conclusion: A Vision for the Future 

 Microeconomies offer a glimpse into a future where value creation is decentralized, inclusive, and driven by community participation. They present an opportunity to redefine our understanding of work, value, and economic participation. As we navigate a world marked by economic uncertainty and technological evolution, embracing the concept of microeconomies could be crucial in building a more equitable and dynamic future.

 Like I said in a recent podcast episode, too much scale breeds corruption.

title: From Mayo Showers to Media Monopoly: ESPN's Hand in Bowl Mania and the Quest for a True CFB Champion
text:
Beleaguered football fans breathed a sigh of relief with the NCAA announcement of the 12-team playoff bracket that will be implemented next season. The committee has shown it has an innovative bone in its body. Did they finally come to terms with the fact that promotion and sponsorships have led us to our first edible mascot, and bathing coaches in various snack items you might find being passed out at your son's little league football game?

 Although the league is moving in the right direction, we are still leaving teams ranked 13-25 with very little reward for a successful season. Why have a top 25 and only have 12-teams compete in the playoffs?

 As a sport that ranks 2 nd domestically and in the top five by viewership worldwide, it's time to put some respect on college football. College football is a final destination for many athletes, some because of the institution of NIL have the ability to make a living without ever stepping foot on an NFL football field. These programs are the front porch of their universities and bring in more revenue for their institutions than any other sport on campus. With attendance rates doubling that of all professional leagues other than the NFL, fans deserve a more competitive and inclusive top-tier college football landscape.

 It is time to have a 24-team tournament bracket to crown a FBS national champion. The 24-team CFB bracket pictured above could rival March Madness and be the most televised and viewed sports program over the course of five weeks, starting in December. Fans of sports watch tournaments  even when their teams aren’t in them because of the drama, excitement and unpredictability. 

 While CFB traditionalists maintain an unwavering connection to the bowl season, the athletes have shown they need something bigger to fight for. Some teams treat their bowl games like a casual picnic, and the star players on teams invited to the less popular bowls have been known to decline the game invitation to prepare for NFL opportunities. A 60 point victory margin over one of the best teams in the country was caused by players from Florida State opting out of playing Georgia in the Orange bowl. FSU players saw little reason to play a "pointless" bowl game.

 Other notable players who skipped their bowl games this year, including but not limited to:

 QB: Jayden Daniels* (LSU), Drake Maye (UNC), Taulia Tagovailoa (Maryland), Caleb Williams (USC), Michael Pratt (Tulane), Joe Milton III (Tennessee)

 WR: Marvin Harrison Jr. (OSU), Troy Franklin (Oregon)

 TE: Brock Bowers (Georgia)

 OL/DL: Chop Robinson (DE, PSU), Olu Fashanu (OL PSU), Jackson Powers-Johnson (OL, Oregon)

 * Heisman Trophy winner

 The bowl game family has gotten quite large with a total of 43 bowl games played in the month of December (See chart below). We have nearly doubled the number of bowl games since the turn of the millennium.

 

 

 The biggest thing from these new bowl games are the celebration showers where winning teams upgraded from dumping Gatorade on their coaches heads to dumping things like French Fries, Frosted Flakes, Mayonnaise, Eggnog, and Cheez-Its. We even had a winning team eat the Pop-Tart bowl mascot (See video).

 

 How does this exponential growth make sense when very few are satisfied with the current setup? You might not realize this, but ESPN has slowly built a monopoly on the bowl game season. Out of 43 bowl games, ESPN/ABC family networks (both owned by Disney) shared coverage of all but three bowl games this season; the only exceptions being the Tony the Tiger Sun Bowl on CBS, The DIRECTV Holiday Bowl on FOX, and the Arizona Bowl on CW Network and Barstool.

 ESPN is the only guaranteed beneficiary from these low level bowl games. They use these games to fill down time slots in their broadcast. This is akin to Netflix paying for mid-tier shows with cult-like audiences to bolster their library. ESPN's interest runs even deeper...did you know ESPN owns 13 bowl games outright? The number of games began to skyrocket shortly after ESPN purchased its first bowl game in 2001. As you can see, the exponential growth of bowl games is correlated with ESPN's buying spree and monopolization of the bowl game broadcasts.

 The question is, are these lower level games profitable for anyone other than ESPN? The New Year's Six bowl games have consistently earned tens of millions in revenue but the rest show no guarantee in profitable outcomes for teams, in fact many teams have lost money. So, what do these programs with the status of the University riding on its back play for each year? A record of random bowl wins, where they may or may not make any money and their best players may or may not participate.

 So, here is our idea fleshed out: a 24-team tournament, 8 automatic bids and first round byes from the teams competing in the remaining Power Five conference championships: SEC, Big Ten, ACC and Big 12. The rest of the teams should be filled in based on the top 25 rankings. Keep the tradition of the New Year's Six bowl games by rotating them throughout the games held in the 3rd and 4th rounds leading up to the national championship.

 The current bowl/playoff system lacks a true hunt for the trophy. Even though the 4 teams that made the BCS playoffs in 2023 were great competitors, we failed Florida St, we failed Georgia and we failed the Pac-12. Is the current bowl game set-up partially to blame for the collapse of a Power Five conference? Could the Pac-12 have been saved? With the collapse of the Pac-12, the future of the Big 12 at stake and Florida State suing the ACC, are we looking at a future with 2 super-conferences? 

 Kirby Smart, Georgia HC on the need for change:

 “People need to look at what happened tonight, and they need to fix this[…]. Everybody is saying we had our guys, [Florida State] didn’t have their guys. I can listen to all that, but college football has gotta decide what they want. And I know things are changing, and how things are gonna change next year. But you know what? There’s still going to be bowl games outside of [the playoff]. People need to decide what they want and what they wanna get out of it. It’s really unfortunate for those kids on that sideline that had to play in that game that didn’t have their full arsenal. It affected the game, 100%.”

 — https://twitter.com/geoppls/status/1742939487322177709 

 

 
A big thank you to Megan Skinner for helping me with this article. ❤️

title: How Messi's Next Gen Jordan Deal Ushers In A New Era for Major League Soccer
text:
Since the inception of the Designated Player rule that brought David Beckham to Major League Soccer (MLS) in 2007, the league has made significant strides in attracting sports fans in the U.S, establishing itself alongside the country's 'Big Four' pro sports. However, with soccer being the global spectacle that it is, MLS still has some distance to cover before it can stand toe-to-toe with prominent leagues like the UK's Premier League or Spain’s LaLiga. The landscape is poised for a seismic shift as MLS is making global headlines with the entrance of superstar Lionel Messi, arguably the greatest soccer player of all time, to Inter Miami.

 The interest surrounding Inter Miami has intensified following a sports contract with Messi that has never been seen before. Despite an alleged jaw-dropping offer of $400 million per year from Saudi Arabia, Messi chose to embrace a less conventional, but just as unprecedented offer from Inter Miami. He is taking a different route than his GOAT rival Cristiano Ronaldo, who signed with the Saudi Pro league for $200 million a year. 

 Rather than matching the enormous salary, Inter Miami, in collaboration with Apple and Adidas, presented an innovative package. Apple, the holder of MLS's streaming rights, offered Messi a slice of streaming revenue if he brings in international subscribers, a first in sports history. With a share in streaming revenues from Apple, a cut of MLS apparel sales from Adidas, and a future stake in Inter Miami, Messi's deal underscores his belief in the potential of the MLS and the value he can add both on and off the field. 

 This unique arrangement is reminiscent of Michael Jordan's groundbreaking deal with Nike, a partnership that propelled him to billionaire status. These generational deals don’t come often, and I don’t expect to see another one anytime soon. Messi’s draw is unlike any other athlete in the world’s stardom. * Within a week of his trade announcement, Inter Miami's Instagram account saw a surge in followers, gaining a staggering seven million. 

 

 

 His on-field impact is equally impressive. Messi marked his debut with a magical match-winning penalty kick at the end of stoppage time, which was the perfect beginning to a potential Cinderella season for Inter Miami. With incentives aligned, Messi seems to be doing what he can to give Inter Miami a real chance at a championship, and he understands you can’t win a championship in a team sport with one person.

 

 Messi has a gravitational pull, and he has not come to Miami alone; he's brought with him ex Barcelona and Argentina coach Gerardo Martino, as well as his former Barcelona teammates Sergio Busquets and Jordi Alba. The impact of Messi's move is also reverberating beyond Miami. It's rumored that another ex-teammate, Luis Suarez, is looking to make a move to Florida. Suarez, who willingly signed a two-year contract with Brazilian club Gremio at the beginning of the year, has renegotiated his contract to expire at the end of the year, keeping the door open for a potential reunion with Messi. Even the official Argentina Football Federation is planning to expand in Miami. The initial signs are promising. Inter Miami won every single game since Messi’s debut, and they’re set to compete in the Leagues Cup Final this Saturday.

 Messi's move involves a critical mass of talent that could have implications for the quality and style of football in the MLS. Criticism of the league's tactics and understanding of modern football concepts such as possession-based attacks, pressing, and counter-pressing, is not new. Football analyst Stephen A. Smith equates the MLS to a "G-league compared to soccer in Europe." Many MLS teams still adhere to a style of play reminiscent of English football two to three decades ago, focusing on long balls and capitalizing on defensive errors rather than strategizing intricate attacks. This, mixed with MLS’s history of competitive balance , may be the perfect storm that allows Inter Miami to climb the ranks for a potential playoff run.

 Thanks for reading Innovative Hype! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

 

 

 

 Messi's arrival might just be the catalyst needed to take MLS to the next level, however, the journey won’t be easy. Messi's move to the MLS follows a tradition of top players joining the league in their later career years, with varying degrees of success. As Wayne Rooney, ex-player and manager of DC United FC, noted, previous superstars have struggled to maintain their commitment to the MLS, often leaving or retiring within a couple of years. Only one international player in MLS history has transferred into a club and won the MLS cup in the same year, and that team was at the top of their conference. But Messi's influence, owing to his unparalleled footballing skills that led Argentina to a world cup win just last year, coupled with the incentives baked into his contract, could transcend those who preceded him.

 The task is massive for Messi and crew. And the clock is ticking. Messi's contract is set to expire in 2025, coinciding with the completion of Inter Miami's new stadium. 

 Can Messi convert a new continent into his fans, convince people who call soccer “football” that MLS is worth watching, drive millions of subscribers for MLS Season Pass, and at the same time bring a languishing club at the bottom of their conference to win their first MLS cup title? Even on the biggest stage, Messi continues to amaze me. 

 Messi's move to Inter Miami is more than just a transfer. Just like David Beckham’s move to LA Galaxy marked a new era for MLS, it’s likely that this generational deal leads to a new era in MLS as well. With the eyes of the world now firmly on MLS, the next few years promise to be a thrilling ride for all stakeholders. 

 Thank you for reading Innovative Hype. This post is public so feel free to share it.

title: Making Music In Public
text:
Aaand we're back!
I'm finally done with #gpplsDaily. Play the best on Spotify. 
So I've started a daily writing habit. 
Just like gpplsDaily except with writing, if you want to get a behind the scenes look of my "medium-rare mind," learn more here. 

 

 At the DIY Musician conference I had a great conversation about the how the music making process is becoming more transparent because of the internet with Dan Arwady from YouTube. I told him I make a song every day.

 Last October I started an experiment where I made a song and published it every day for 365 days. I mainly did it as a way to catch up since hadn’t rapped or produced in years. I crowdsourced song topics, beats to trap over, and livestreamed myself freestyling and writing songs, and making beats. I have a lot of ideas for Twitch/interactive music making. We have seen subtle versions of this before.

 He mentioned how people in the younger generation, like my age—because in his early 30s—are more likely to upload more raw music and share it. He talked about how people get to see your process and see you improve over time and that’s authenticity.

 And authenticity is hugely valuable. It’s a large part of your brand as an artist. I told him people want to see behind the scenes of musicians they like. So it makes sense to share more than just the most polished high-quality end result. It also makes sense to share things that are more early, unfinished. Share your process. Maybe give your fans an opportunity to interact and influence the end result.

 How much value could sharing your process bring? If you ever thought about writing a book, check out Ryan Holiday’s writeup on how he wrote The Perennial Seller .

 Dan said back in his day labels and management teams would push the artist to polish it completely and never send an unfinished product.

 This made me realize the dichotomy. The traditional, solo, Bon Iver style deep work creative purist method is on one side. The 21st century Internet enabled twitch/live stream fan-engaged loose, open-ended recording session is on the other side.

 Also, movies get pre-screened. Why shouldn’t your songs? Industry studio sessions often have multiple songwriters collaborating. Why shouldn’t you have writing collaborators? This doesn’t have to be public. 

 DIY musicians should realize this is their competitive advantage. Embrace making in the open. Livestreaming is only second to in person interactions as far as intimacy and community building goes.

 The least fun part of making a song or publishing in my newsletter every day is doing it alone. The creative process doesn’t have to be a solo quest like quest love talked about performing with no audience

 I secretly hope creating out in the open will help me find other prolific creatives to proliferate with.

title: My 2019 DIY Musician Conference Experience
text:
I’m paying attention to what platforms artists are connecting on. The first artist I met, Brooklyn Michelle, looked me up on Spotify then we immediately connected on instagram.

 It’s vital to capture potential fans and track engagement granularly enough for retargeting. Facebook is their platform of choice. 
 
 The biggest issues they’ve seen with clients is not nurturing your fan relationship and not making enough offers.

 If you’re looking for more valuable from them check out their podcast 

 

 I had an great convo about private vs public music making with Daniel Arwady from YouTube . I told him about  #gpplsDaily  and how I create in the open ever day, much of it being rough/unpolished. He noted how people get to see my process growth over time. That’s authenticity.

 Back when he came up as a musician, your manager, label or whoever’s overseeing your work would push you to polish it completely and never send an unfinished product. This made me realize the dichotomy.

 The private vs public music making dichotomy
 
 The traditional solo Bon Iver style deep work creative purist method is on one side. 
 The 21st century Internet enabled twitch live stream fan engaged loose open ended recording session is on the other side.

 

 

 Loved how real and open Questlove and Jaxta CEO’s chat was was. 

 “Embrace boredom. That’s where the deepest creativity comes from.”
 
Miyamoto, creator of many Nintendo classics, cited nature as the primary catalyst for his creativity. He grew up near mountains in japan

 “We live in a post remote control highlight reel era where people want to see the the end result and don’t want to see what went into it” 
 
 Patreon, Discord, Twitch etc. are underrated. We’ll see the mainstream shift from discovery to membership platforms over the next decade.

 Questlove used to write 26 pg liner notes for The Roots albums explaining the backstory of songs. He stopped after they started limiting the length. He grew up in a 5k record household where you would put in headphones and get lost in a record, reading liner notes. Times changed.

 A theme in the Q&A was, how do we keep the spirit of the iconic influencers of music alive? J Dilla, Nujabes, Jimmy Hendrix, Aretha Franklin.
 
 “Pharrell and Dilla are the main people who treated their creativity as a profession.”
 
 Take creativity seriously.
 Be influenced by them.

 I’ve been a huge advocate for live streaming on twitch of course as I do so myself is when  @askmikewarner  told me there was someone writing a book about twitch for musicians I had to meet her!
 

 So this happened...
 . #diymusician #startlivestreaming @MicahPpls 

 A Spotify playlist hack
 
 When you’re not on Rap Caviar, 20 artist picks are better than one.
 
 A rapper was disappointed he wasn’t on rap caviar, but had 20 artists he toured with. They made a playlist with tracks from each and all made it their artist pick.
 It got 10k followers.

 There were a ton more sessions but I couldn’t catch them all! I’ll be looking forward to seeing some recorded sessions on  @cdbaby ’s youtube. Until then, it was a blast volunteering with  @rpsmusic . I met some wonderful people, and i’m looking forward to the next conference!

title: It’s Your Fault You Don’t Have a Direct Relationship with Your Fans
text:
Innovative Hype is back! Outside of gppls daily, my project to make a song a day for a year, I've decluttered my life a bit in my quest to become the Zen Adult. So, you should be seeing this banner☝🏾in your inbox more often (: 

 

 I listened to a great interview with Cherie Hu and Sammy Andrews on the Water and Music podcast titled “ The music business needs to break down its own data silos ” . They discuss different data silos in the music industry and acknowledge the importance of that data for retargeting and community building. They suggest the best way to protect artists is to ensure that they can have their consumption, audience, and payment data move with them. 

 Here’s a bullet from the episode’s webpage (linked above) that summarized the idea I’m tackling in this piece:

 “Data silos prevent artists from being able to treat themselves as legitimate, always-on brands.” 

 In this piece I’ll explain why artists can’t rely on digital service providers (DSPs) for this data, why you’d want to reward your fans, and how you could go about building a strong artist brand/community.

 Artists Can’t Rely on DSPs

 DSPs, particularly streaming platforms, control the end user experience and are in control of your relationship with your fans, so they have all the data. They know the demographics of your fan base; their names, what city they live in, which songs they listen to the most, how much of a song they listen to. And you as the artist only get a small subset of that data.

 Cherie and Sammy discuss how audience data should move with the artist. Allowing the content creators that drive engagement on their platform to drive engagement somewhere else, doesn’t seem like a lucrative opportunity for a public company with a shareholder’s bottom line. Data is the new oil, so of course they'll be protective of it. And with privacy grievances galore, they have good reason to. Besides, they are the ones with the leverage. If they were to provide zero audience data, it would still be worthwhile to be on the platform. And your music is replaceable. In the same way people get on Netflix and then find something to watch, many Spotify users listen to playlists in the background and pay no mind to half the artists they hear. This is why you want to build an ecosystem and community around your work.  

 Music is an individual experience to an extent. And as artists we have to put our music into the ether, like dandelion seeds, and let it percolate. But how do you reward your fans for being more engaged? If you have the technology to give our fans a deeper relationship with you and your art, why wouldn’t you use it? 

 Rewarding Fans and Building Community

 Sammy and Cherie highlight how Taylor Swift and Ticketmaster’s pay-to-play debacle where fans were forced to purchase her music and merch to get a better chance at getting tickets to her show. This use of bundling tries to squeeze the amount a superfan would happily fork from a regular fan. This is the wrong way to go about rewarding fans. Instead of making fans feel like crabs in a bucket, fighting for the default opportunity, provide additional perks and put fans who take advantage of it on a pedestal. If you simply put out merch and identify who made purchases, you could easily give those fans a reward or incentive.

 While other artists are dependent on promotion, you should instead lean into your brand and community. Promotion is done through media. You are a media entity and must develop a direct channel to your fans whether it’s a community, email list, YouTube channel or other form of media. Because when you build your brand/community, you are more likely to have superfans, also known as true fans. And as Kevin Kelly says, you only need 1,000 for a sustainable career. 

 There are many ways you can achieve this. To create regular engagement, you could try to be prolific and like, make a song a day or something idk. Part of why I’m sending this email is for the very reasons we’re discussing. The ability to access and draw on our assets is what makes an artist successful over the long term. There’s a reason Casey Neistat left his film industry successes to build his YouTube channel. Additionally, being an early adopter of an emerging platform like Tik-Tok or Twitch could make growing your base easier. * 

 And if you really want to minimize the likelihood of someone taking your platform away from you, an email list works great. When Kevin Hart started out, he did the comedy club circuit 4 years in a row, and at every show, he got email addresses from audience members by leaving cards on each table with the message “Kevin Hart needs to know who you are”. His assistant would log all the email addresses in a spreadsheet organized by city, so the next time Kevin was performing there, he would reach out to every person individually to invite them to his show. This personal touch helped to sell out his shows and build a loyal fan base that follows him to this day.

 Another way to think about this is you want to create an ecosystem around your work that forms a new world for your listeners to explore and run away to. * Remember becausetheinter.net ? The domain is no longer active, but it transformed the Because the Internet album into a larger narrative you could experience, accompanied by a short film and visuals throughout the screenplay. It would be great if Spotify did this work for us, but they have a laundry list of features that contribute to their bottom line to get to first. We can’t rely on streaming platforms to do even a fraction of that for the artists they profit from.

 Moreover, in the future you won’t be famous for 15 minutes, you’ll be famous to 15 people. This relates well to a saying by one of my favorite marketers. Nik Sharma says community trumps quantity . In this sense, the deeper engagement of a smaller community in, say your discord server, trumps a greater number of people streaming your single on Spotify. Streaming platforms just don’t provide these affordances right now.

 Granted, for Apple Music subscribers you could use Apple Music Connect. But that’s platform specific, and lots of music lovers aren’t aware it exists. An alternative would be a Facebook group, twitter, or a slack/discord server. This would allow you to have conversations, do polls, reward people with high engagement, etc. Building community is especially important if you focus on growing digitally (not doing many shows) as I have. 

 And at that point all you’d need to worry about is finding who purchases your merch (and if you don’t have merch, get some! ). Superphone is a fine solution to this, but isn’t artist focused. The homie @only1Swami on twitter is working on another solution and hopefully he’ll give us a sneak peak. Be on the lookout for the gppls daily app that is in development, to see cultivating that direct relationship in action. In the meantime, listen to a few gppls daily favorites . (;

 Stay Frosty ✌🏾

 

 * Potential topic for a following newsletter. Let me know if any in particular piques your interest.

 P.S. Shoutout to @alexbhlz , @only1Swami , @ohhmissmarie for providing feedback on my writing.

 Some of these views were shaped by The Perennial Seller by Ryan Holiday, a book I’d recommend to all artists.

title: Audio-First Spotify and The Ever Increasing Space of Audio
text:
2008 - Music

 2018 - Podcasts

 2028 - Listen to any article from the web?

 Spotify’s goal is to own audio. Currently, the space of audio consists of music, podcasts, and radio. If Spotify is successful in owning this space, their valuation will be massive.

 The space of audio won’t only contain music, podcasts, and radio though. As text to speech synthesis improves and becomes less robotic and more natural sounding, we are able to switch between reading and listening to articles seamlessly. I wouldn’t doubt that Spotify will come for web articles too.

 Imagine a day when you’re at the office doing deep work. Someone sends you a couple of articles you can’t read right now. So you save them for later. When you hop in your whip to dip, you press play and start listening to all those articles you saved.

 The best example of an app that is currently doing this is Pocket, the chrome extension that lets you save any web page for later. And if you use their mobile app, you can listen to any article you saved. They use an Amazon service, Amazon Polly, for text to speech synthesis.

 Daniel Ek on Spotify's mission to be audio-first:

 “To really understand, take the current value of the video industry. Consumers spend roughly the same amount of time on video as they do on audio. Video is about a trillion dollar market. And the music and radio industry is worth around a hundred billion dollars. I always come back to the same question: Are our eyes really worth 10 times more than our ears? I firmly believe this is not the case. For example, people still spend over two hours a day listening to radio — and we want to bring that radio listening to Spotify, where we can deepen engagement and create value in new ways. With the world focused on trying to reduce screen time, it opens up a massive audio opportunity.” 

 In preparation for this article, I asked a few friends for their thoughts on this matter. One of them asked a compelling question: Why isn’t there already a company that allows you to listen to podcasts and music in the same playlist?

 Let’s start by answering this first question: What mobile app lets you listen to both music and podcasts? Spotify is currently the only app with this functionality that I know of. While they haven’t introduced playlists with both music and podcasts--and I doubt they will, cuz they’d probably opt for a more personalized and automated experience that resembles traditional radio--let’s give Spotify some credit. They’re not just sitting on the sidelines, waiting for someone else to figure out what type of listening experience their users want. Spotify is at the forefront of audio innovation.

 Now, back to answering the original question--why isn’t there already a company that allows you to listen to podcasts and music in the same playlist? Answer: Big companies move slowly.

 Spotify may not seem like a big company because they have fewer employees than the traditional incumbents of yesteryear and a higher revenue per employee, but recent news of them reaching 100 million paid users, solidifies them as a top dog. Thinking about other tech giants, like Apple and how they’re still behind Spotify, after being the first to have a dedicated podcast app, it’s unlikely they’ll surpass the efforts made by Spotify to truly own audio. Not to mention their apps are only accessible to Apple users. Part of Spotify’s approach is to be universal...with their approach to music. They have realized that exclusivity doesn’t work with music (Cc: Tidal). And this is apparent from a recent Spotify (NYSE: SPOT) earnings call. It should be noted though, as Ek (co-founder and CEO of Spotify)  mentioned on their Q4 2018 earnings call, Spotify’s approach to podcasts will be more of a Netflix-style approach. And though he didn’t use those exact words, their recent Spotify exclusive audio shows, like The Joe Budden Podcast and Amy Schumer Presents: 3 Girls, 1 Keith, put their new strategy on display.

 *smooth transition*

 Why do big companies move slowly though? On an episode of Indie Hackers, Courtland (the host) asked how AJ (a solo founder with a project called Carrd that generates $30,000/mo in revenue) balances feature requests with his product roadmap.

 “If you’re too open and just go with what your users want, you’ll end up with an incoherent mess of features that don’t really fit together. You’ll have niche features for very specific users that don’t have a general use-case” 

 Spotify has a roadmap, and we’re all ready to see what’s next. My guess is if they continue on their current trajectory, they’ll own podcasts by 2028 and as text-to-speech synthesis becomes significantly more advanced, we might just see Spotify come for web articles too.

 

 I’d love to have a conversation about this or get feedback on my writing.

 Feel free to @ or DM me on Twitter  @micahppls .

 Shout out to my editor  @ohhmissmarie  on Twitter.
